simple: Code that other people run and rely on, so its mistakes become their problems.
analogy: The house a family lives in, not the shed you built for yourself.
precise: Software whose behaviour other people or programs depend on without reading its source; it needs a stated interface, a version, failure-path tests, CI, release notes, a known-issues list, a licence record, monitoring and someone who answers when it breaks (this university's working definition, from the BR-09 bridge card).

simple: The way a program goes when something is wrong with its input or its world.
analogy: What the house does when the wind blows, not on a calm day.
precise: Every branch that handles invalid input, an unavailable resource or an out-of-range result, including exceptions thrown but never caught; tested when a test drives the program into it and checks the exact outcome (exit status, message, return value).

simple: A program that behaves correctly only on the computer where it was written.
analogy: A shed that stands straight only because your own garden is flat.
precise: A defect whose visibility depends on the environment rather than the code alone (compiler and version, flags, installed libraries, current directory, locale, environment variables); cured by removing the dependence or adding the difference to the CI matrix.
source: R4, R5, R7 of BR-09 (lab runs); F2-26 forensic lab

simple: C++ does not say which argument of a function call is computed first.
analogy: Two carpenters told to fetch a plank each; the order they come back is not part of the instruction.
precise: The evaluations of the arguments of one function call are indeterminately sequenced with respect to each other, so a result that depends on their order may differ between conforming compilers (g++ 13.3 and clang 18.1 differ in BR-09's run R4, without a warning).

simple: Something the author knew about how the code must be used but never wrote down or checked.
analogy: "Lift the door when it rains", known only to the builder.
precise: A condition on inputs, environment or output format that code relies on and that is neither stated in its interface documentation nor enforced by a check; users discover it by failure.

simple: A three-part version number whose parts tell users whether an update can break them.
analogy: The handover letter says "repairs only", "a new room added", or "the doors moved".
precise: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: MAJOR for changes incompatible with the documented public interface, MINOR for backward-compatible additions, PATCH for backward-compatible fixes; 0.y.z is initial development with no stability promise.
source: D6 (Semantic Versioning 2.0.0) of BR-09 (pending verification); not yet in the source registry

simple: A change after which some existing user's code or script stops working or gives different results.
analogy: Moving a door the family already walks through in the dark.
precise: A change to observable behaviour a caller may depend on: signatures, return types, accepted inputs, output format, exit statuses, error texts scripts match; requires a new MAJOR version under semantic versioning.
source: R13 of BR-09 (lab run); D6 (pending verification)

simple: Old code that used your library still compiles and still means the same with the new version.
analogy: The family's furniture still fits through the new doors.
precise: Every program that compiled against the old public headers compiles against the new ones with the same meaning; differs from binary (ABI) compatibility, where already-compiled programs keep working without recompiling.
source: R12 of BR-09 (lab run: 0.1 tests against 1.0.0)

simple: The list, kept with the code, of what changed in each version and what it means for users.
precise: A file with one entry per released version, newest first, giving version, date, compatibility impact, and what was changed, fixed and added; its newest version can be checked against the build's by a script.

simple: A public list of problems the authors already know about, with workarounds.
analogy: The snag list handed over with the keys.
precise: A maintained document with one identified entry per known defect or limitation, each with effect, who is affected, status and workaround, and where possible a test that pins today's behaviour so a fix shows up as a changed test result.

simple: The conditions under which you may use, change and pass on someone else's code.
analogy: The conditions written on drawings you borrowed from another builder.
precise: The legal terms granted by the copyright holder; open-source licences differ in what they require when code is copied or distributed. BR-09 teaches the engineering habit (record origin and licence, let the owner decide), not the law.
source: C1 (curriculum 5.3 and runbook 19.2) and D8 of BR-09 (pending verification)

simple: A short standard name for a licence, written in a comment at the top of a file.
analogy: The stamp on each borrowed drawing saying whose it is and on what terms.
precise: A line SPDX-License-Identifier: <id> using an identifier from the SPDX License List, or a LicenseRef- identifier for licences not on it, readable by tools.
source: D7 (SPDX specification) of BR-09 (pending verification); not yet in the source registry; R14

simple: A list saying where every copied file came from and under which licence.
analogy: A note: "hinges from Kofi, his permission asked on this date".
precise: One line per copied file with path, origin (project, version, path), SPDX licence and SHA-256 of the copy, so that an unknown origin and a silent local change are both detectable; the data form of curriculum runbook rule 19 ("recording the origin").

simple: The list of everything your shipped program needs that you did not write.
analogy: Which batch of hinges went into which house, so a recall reaches the right doors.
precise: The libraries linked at build time or loaded at run time, the toolchain that built the program, and their versions; the input to deciding which security updates concern you.
source: R17 of BR-09 (lab run: ldd, dpkg-query)

simple: A new version released to close a weakness someone could abuse.
analogy: A hinge recall: the old hinge can be forced open.
precise: A release of your code or of something in your dependency inventory that fixes a vulnerability; implies knowing your dependencies, being able to release quickly, and telling users what to update and why.

simple: An automatic message to a person when too many runs fail.
analogy: The damp meter in the basement that beeps before the floor rots.
precise: A monitoring rule that counts outcomes of a program in use (here by exit status and stable error code), computes the failure fraction over a window and notifies someone above a threshold or on any unclassified failure.
source: D2 of BR-09 (pending verification); R18, R19

simple: How many wrong results a bug produces before everyone has the fix.
analogy: How many nights the family sleeps under the leaking roof before it is mended.
precise: Users × runs per user per day × days from release until the last user has updated × fraction of runs whose input triggers the bug; detection and update time are the factors engineering can shrink.
source: R20 of BR-09 (lab run of exposure.cpp)
